findings.evidence: routes.js:55-59 takes `const overrides = ctx.request.body || {}` and enqueues `{ ...previous.data, ...overrides, retryOf: previous.id }`. No schema is applied - contrast the submit path at line 18, which calls schema.validateRenderJob, and the export path at line 66, which calls schema.validateExportJob. Every constraint the schema module enforces is therefore optional on this route: the documentId pattern, the template enum, the width bounds, checkFilename, and - most consequentially - the ASSET_HOSTS allowlist that validateRenderJob applies to assetBaseUrl (schema.js:74-81). Because overrides is spread LAST it also overwrites tenantId and requestedBy, which the submit path takes from ctx.state.user (routes.js:22-23).
findings.impact: Any authenticated user, starting from one job they legitimately own, enqueues a job with arbitrary field values: assetBaseUrl pointing anywhere (which is F-OJ-02), tenantId set to another tenant so the artifact is written under that tenant's prefix (render.js:64), and template or width outside their declared domains. The ownership check at routes.js:51 validates the job being copied, not the job being created.
findings.recommendation: Run the merged object through schema.validateRenderJob before enqueueing, and re-pin tenantId and requestedBy from ctx.state.user AFTER the spread so a body field cannot displace them. Better still, accept an explicit allowlist of retryable fields rather than a merge.

triage.reason: The validating layer exists in the same module and is simply not called on this path - schema.validateRenderJob is invoked at routes.js:18 and not at line 56.
overrides is ctx.request.body in full, parsed by koa-bodyparser with no schema between it and the queue.
The overridable attributes include tenantId, which is the tenant-isolation field, and assetBaseUrl, which is the SSRF-relevant one - both have direct security impact.

findings.title: The render worker fetches the asset manifest from a job-supplied base URL
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs render worker fetches job.data.assetBaseUrl
findings.evidence: render.js:50-51 takes `job.data.assetBaseUrl` and calls fetchAssetManifest, which fetches `${baseUrl}/manifest.json` (line 21) with no host, scheme or address check in the worker itself. The only allowlist in the system is in the API at schema.js:74-81, and F-OJ-01 shows the retry route reaches enqueueRender without it. The worker therefore treats the queue payload as trusted - the comment at export.js:29-30 states that assumption for the sibling processor in as many words - while one of the two producers does not validate.
findings.impact: A request originating from the worker's network position, which is the position that holds the S3 credentials and the Redis connection: the cloud metadata endpoint, internal services, and anything reachable from the worker subnet. The fetched body is parsed as JSON and its `css` field is then interpolated into the rendered page (F-OJ-03), so the response is not discarded.
findings.recommendation: Re-validate assetBaseUrl against ASSET_HOSTS inside the processor rather than trusting the producer - the queue is a trust boundary and both sides of it should enforce. Resolve the host and reject non-public addresses, and disable redirect following.

triage.reason: The allowlist that would be the compensating control is bypassable on the retry path (F-OJ-01), so the control does not cover every path to the sink - which is exactly what FP-01 requires.
The value originates in a request body and reaches the worker through the queue unchanged.
The intended outbound call is to three named asset hosts (schema.js:7-11); nothing bounds the actual call to them on this path.

findings.title: A value from the fetched manifest is interpolated into the HTML rendered by a sandbox-less Chromium
findings.class: HTML injection into a privileged renderer
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs render interpolates manifest.css into an attribute, and chromium runs --no-sandbox
findings.evidence: render.js:55-60 writes the page with `href="${baseUrl}/${manifest.css}"` - manifest.css comes from the JSON body fetched at line 27, which per F-OJ-02 an attacker can serve. It is interpolated into a double-quoted attribute with no escaping, so a value containing a double quote closes the attribute and injects markup. The other two interpolations are constrained (documentId matches ^[a-f0-9]{24}$ per schema.js:22, templateFile comes from the TEMPLATES map at lines 14-18), which leaves manifest.css as the one free position. The page is then loaded from file:// by chromium-headless with --no-sandbox (render.js:34), i.e. attacker-influenced markup rendered by a browser process with the OS sandbox disabled, whose output becomes the customer-facing PDF. Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule invoked on this finding is answered UNKNOWN, and an UNKNOWN caps a finding at probable; the code relationship itself is established, and what is unsettled is named in the triage block.
findings.impact: Injected markup and script into a document rendered from a file:// origin by an unsandboxed browser, and into the PDF that is then published (F-OJ-04). The renderer process runs with the worker's privileges and no sandbox, so a Chromium vulnerability that the sandbox would contain is not contained.
findings.recommendation: Escape or, better, validate manifest.css against a strict filename pattern before interpolating; remove --no-sandbox and give the container the seccomp profile Chromium needs instead.

triage.reason: manifest.css is a field of a JSON document fetched from a URL the job payload controls; no validation is applied to the parsed object.

What the injected markup achieves inside a headless render-to-PDF pass is not fully established from this tree - chromium restricts file:// subresource reads, so local file exfiltration is not demonstrated, while markup and styling injection into the output document plainly is. Per triage.md this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable-strength certainty and is why confidence is medium and severity is medium rather than high.
No escaping or templating layer sits between the value and the file: fs.writeFile receives a template literal.

findings.title: Rendered customer documents are uploaded with a public-read ACL and a guessable address
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs render uploads with public:true
findings.evidence: render.js:64 builds the key as `${tenantId}/renders/${documentId}.pdf` and lines 68-71 call storage.putObject with `public: true`, which storage.js:39 turns into `ACL: 'public-read'` and line 40 into a year-long public cache header. The returned artifact URL is storage.publicUrl (line 75), an unsigned `${PUBLIC_BASE}/${key}`. The comment at lines 66-67 gives the reason - the document is linked from a customer e-mail and needs an address that does not expire - so the choice is deliberate and its consequence is not: documentId is a 24-hex-character identifier and tenantId is a short slug (schema.js:35), so the whole key space is enumerable by anyone who learns a tenant slug.
findings.impact: Every rendered invoice, statement and letter is world-readable to anyone who has or guesses the URL, with no authentication and no expiry. These are per-customer financial documents.
findings.recommendation: Upload with ACL private and hand out genuine time-limited pre-signed URLs (the AWS SDK's getSignedUrl, not the scheme in F-OJ-05). If a non-expiring link is a hard requirement for e-mail, mint a per-document capability token stored server-side and serve the object through an endpoint that checks it.

triage.reason: The intended exposure is one document to one recipient; public-read on a guessable key exposes every document to everyone, so the exposure is not bounded to the intent. Per FP-05 the finding stays and points at what sits behind the intended exposure.
The objects are invoices and statements rendered per customer - personal and financial data.
No bucket policy or block-public-access setting in this repository counteracts the object ACL; storage.js sets the ACL directly and nothing else configures the bucket.

findings.title: Artifact URL signatures are minted and never verified, and the scheme is a raw hash rather than an HMAC
findings.class: control declared but never enforced / weak construction
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs verifySignedUrl has no callers and objectSignature is not an HMAC
findings.evidence: Two defects in one mechanism. (1) A call-site enumeration for verifySignedUrl returns the declaration at storage.js:65 and the export at line 78 - nothing calls it. signedUrl IS called, at routes.js:76, so the system mints tokens and never checks one; the expiry test at line 66 and the constant-time comparison at line 70 are code that never runs. (2) objectSignature (lines 51-56) is `sha256(secret || key || expiresAt)` - a raw hash of a secret prefix, not an HMAC, so it is exposed to length-extension, and the three inputs are concatenated with no delimiter, so a (key, expiresAt) pair is ambiguous with a different pair that concatenates to the same string.
findings.impact: The private-artifact link is decorative: an attacker who alters expires or sig is not rejected by anything in this codebase, because nothing consults the signature. Combined with F-OJ-04, which uploads objects as public-read, the endpoint's implied protection does not exist at any layer. The construction weakness matters the moment verification is wired up as written.
findings.recommendation: Either use the AWS SDK's own pre-signed URLs and delete this module, or call verifySignedUrl on the serving path and rebuild objectSignature as crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret) over a delimited, canonical string.

triage.reason: The verifier could in principle live in an edge function outside the repository, but the URL points at PUBLIC_BASE, which storage.js:8 defaults to the raw S3 endpoint - and S3 does not understand an `expires`/`sig` pair of this shape. There is no artifact to credit and the default configuration argues against one.
It cannot be consumed by name: it is a CommonJS export that must be required and called, and no module requires it.
It is not redundant defence in depth - it is the only access control the artifact endpoint implies, and F-OJ-04 shows the layer beneath it is public.

findings.title: The partner webhook enqueues export jobs with an unvalidated tenant and filename
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs webhook export path skips validateExportJob
findings.evidence: webhook.js:46-53 builds the export payload directly from the request body - tenantId from body.tenant_id and filename from body.filename - and calls queue.enqueueExport. It never calls schema.validateExportJob, which the API's own export route uses at routes.js:66 and which enforces the tenant pattern ^[a-z0-9-]{3,40}$ (schema.js:35) and checkFilename's ^(\w+\.)*\w+$ (schema.js:16, 63). The consumer trusts that: export.js:29-30 says "Job payloads reach this queue already validated at submission time", then joins both values into a filesystem path at line 40 - `path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, tenantId, filename + '.' + format)` - and writes to it after mkdir -p on the parent (lines 41-42). path.join resolves `..` rather than rejecting it.
findings.impact: A partner who can produce a valid signature writes files to arbitrary filesystem paths as the worker user - a filename of `../../../../etc/cron.d/x` or a path into an application directory is a write primitive and, given a writable location on an execution path, code execution. Independently, an unvalidated tenantId writes one partner's data into another tenant's export directory and reads the staging file of a tenant of the attacker's choosing (export.js:17).
findings.recommendation: Call schema.validateExportJob on the webhook path exactly as the API route does, and independently re-validate in the processor - canonicalise the target and assert it remains under EXPORT_ROOT before writing, rather than trusting the producer.

triage.reason: The validating layer exists (schema.validateExportJob) and this producer does not call it, while the processor explicitly assumes it was called. Neither side enforces, which is the composition failure.
Both values come from the JSON body with no pattern applied on this path.
A signature-bearing partner is still a second principal relative to the tenants whose directories and staging files it can reach, and relative to the host filesystem.

findings.title: The worker logs the entire job payload on failure, including the caller's callback token
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs worker logs job.data wholesale on failure
findings.evidence: index.js:30-41 logs `payload: job.data` on every failed job, with the comment at lines 28-29 explaining the intent: "Keep the whole payload on failures." job.data for a render job includes callbackToken, which routes.js:26 copies straight from the request body and the comment at line 25 describes as travelling on the completion callback - i.e. a bearer credential for the caller's own endpoint. It also includes documentId and tenantId. Nothing redacts: the pino logger at index.js:10 is constructed with a name and a level only, no redact option, though pino supports one.
findings.impact: A caller-supplied secret is written in clear text to the log stream on every job failure, and jobs are retried three times by default (queue/index.js:13), so a failing job writes it repeatedly. Anyone with log access - which is a wider set than anyone with queue access - can call the tenant's callback endpoint as the platform.
findings.recommendation: Configure pino's redact option for callbackToken and any future credential field, and log a job identifier plus the fields needed to reproduce rather than the payload wholesale. Keep the full payload, if it is genuinely needed, in a store with the same access controls as the queue.

triage.reason: No redaction layer exists: pino is constructed with {name, level} at index.js:10 and no redact paths, and no serializer strips the field.
callbackToken is a credential by its own naming and by its use - it is sent on the completion callback so the receiver can authenticate the call.
The handler is unconditional and the start:worker script runs with NODE_ENV=production (package.json:9); there is no environment gate on the failure logger.

findings.title: Session tokens carry no expiry and none is checked
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs decodeSession never checks an expiry claim
findings.evidence: server.js:13-33 verifies the HMAC over the payload correctly - a length check followed by crypto.timingSafeEqual at line 26 - then JSON-parses the payload and returns it. No exp, iat or nbf is read, and the middleware at lines 62-74 assigns the result to ctx.state.user unconditionally. There is no server-side session store and no revocation list anywhere in the tree, so the token is the entire state. Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule invoked on this finding is answered UNKNOWN, and an UNKNOWN caps a finding at probable; the code relationship itself is established, and what is unsettled is named in the triage block.
findings.impact: A token captured once is valid for the lifetime of ORCHARD_SESSION_SECRET. There is no logout that can invalidate it and no way to revoke a compromised session short of rotating the secret and signing every user out. The claims include tenantId, which is the tenant-isolation field for every route in routes.js.
findings.recommendation: Include and enforce an expiry claim, and add a revocation list keyed by a session identifier. Alternatively adopt a vetted JWT library with expiry validation on by default rather than a hand-rolled payload.signature format.

triage.reason: No layer bounds the lifetime: there is no session store, no cache and no gateway configuration in this repository.

The service that mints these tokens is not in this tree and might embed and enforce an expiry elsewhere, but this API is the verifier and it performs no such check. Per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS; the finding is on the verification side, which is fully visible here.
With no session store the expiry check is the only mechanism that could end a session, so it is not redundant.

findings.title: The Redis connection falls back to a hardcoded password
findings.unaided_label: orchard-jobs Redis password defaults to a literal
findings.evidence: queue/index.js:5-10 builds the ioredis connection with `password: process.env.REDIS_PASSWORD || 'orchard-local-dev'`. The same object is exported and reused by both workers (worker/index.js:14, 20), so the fallback applies to the API and the worker alike. Unlike storage.js:15, which gates its development endpoint on NODE_ENV, this fallback has no environment gate.
findings.impact: A deployment that omits REDIS_PASSWORD silently authenticates with a value published in this repository. Whoever reaches the Redis port then reads and writes the job queues - injecting export and render jobs, which per F-OJ-06 and F-OJ-02 are themselves powerful primitives. Bounded to low because it requires network access to Redis and a missing environment variable.
findings.recommendation: Fail fast when REDIS_PASSWORD is absent rather than substituting a literal, mirroring storage.js:26-30, which throws when ORCHARD_ARTIFACT_SECRET is missing.

triage.reason: The literal is self-describing as a local development value, which is FP-02's placeholder case, and it bounds the severity to low. It does not delete the finding: unlike a ${VAR} placeholder it is a working credential that produces a successful connection, so the misconfiguration is silent.
There is no environment gate - the same expression is evaluated under NODE_ENV=production, and the sibling storage.js shows the codebase knows how to gate when it wants to.
Exploitation additionally requires network reach to Redis, which nothing in this repository grants. Severity downgraded to low and recorded.

findings.title: The production API task role is granted AdministratorAccess
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk prod apiTier ops maps to AdministratorAccess
findings.evidence: environments.ts:26-30 maps the 'ops' tier to the AWS managed policy AdministratorAccess. prod sets apiTier: 'ops' (line 68) with the comment that the production API also exposes maintenance commands. service-role.ts:43-46 resolves cfg.tierPolicies[cfg.apiTier] and attaches it via ManagedPolicy.fromAwsManagedPolicyName, and api-stack.ts:33-47 makes that role the taskRole of the Fargate task definition. The narrow grants that follow - grantArtifacts, grantQueue, database.secret.grantRead (lines 39-41) - are additive and are subsumed by the managed policy. Note also that dev and staging use the 'standard' tier, which maps to ReadOnlyAccess: an account-wide read of every service, itself far past what the service needs.
findings.impact: Any code execution or SSRF in the production API container yields full administrative control of AWS account 000000000003 - every bucket, every database, every role, and the ability to create new principals for persistence. It converts a single application vulnerability into total account compromise, and the neighbouring services in this tree show that SSRF and code execution are not hypothetical classes here.
findings.recommendation: Delete the tier mechanism and let each stack grant only what its service uses - the three calls at api-stack.ts:39-41 already express that. If break-glass administration is genuinely needed, put it in a separate role assumed by a human with MFA and session logging, never in a task role attached to an internet-facing service.

triage.reason: No condition narrows it - fromAwsManagedPolicyName attaches the policy whole - and no SCP, permission boundary or organizational guardrail is declared anywhere in this repository.
The comment at lines 66-67 bounds the INTENT to maintenance commands; nothing bounds the grant, which covers every action on every resource.

There is no reading under which this is benign: the string 'AdministratorAccess' resolves to the AWS managed policy of that name, and the role is the task role of a running service, not a deployment-time role with a short session.

findings.title: One bucket holds brand assets, rendered documents and tenant exports, and is opened to anonymous readers
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk artifact bucket is public-read in prod and holds tenant exports
findings.evidence: The two halves are in different files, which is what makes it survive a per-file reading. data-stack.ts:26-32 says what the bucket holds: "One bucket holds everything the platform produces: the brand assets the CDN pulls, the rendered documents and the tenant data exports", and passes publicRead: cfg.assetsPublic. environments.ts:65 sets assetsPublic: true for prod (dev too, line 37). bucket.ts:33-39 then replaces BLOCK_ALL with a BlockPublicAccess that sets blockPublicPolicy and restrictPublicBuckets to false, and lines 55-64 attach a resource policy granting s3:GetObject to iam.AnyPrincipal on arnForObjects('*') - every object, not a prefix. The construct's own docstring at lines 16-19 says "Public reads are opt-in", which is true and hides that the opt-in is bucket-wide.
findings.impact: Every rendered customer document and every tenant data export in the production account is readable by anyone on the internet who knows or guesses the key. The intended public surface is the brand assets; the actual public surface is the entire bucket.
findings.recommendation: Split the buckets: one public origin bucket for brand assets, one fully blocked bucket for documents and exports. If they must share, scope the AnyPrincipal statement to arnForObjects('brand/*') and keep blockPublicPolicy true elsewhere - but separate buckets are the control that cannot be defeated by a key-naming mistake.

triage.reason: The intended exposure is the CDN reading brand assets. Per FP-05 the exculpation requires what bounds it, and nothing does: the statement covers '*', and the same bucket receives exports. The finding moves to what sits behind the intended exposure, which is the tenant data.

The recommended control - a CDN origin access identity with the bucket itself blocked, which INF-02 names explicitly - is not used; the policy grants AnyPrincipal directly and the block-public-access settings are relaxed to permit it.
Rendered documents and tenant data exports are customer data, per the data-stack comment that describes the contents.

findings.title: The dev environment opens SSH to the whole internet, and it is the fallback environment
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk dev adminCidrs is 0.0.0.0/0
findings.evidence: environments.ts:36 sets adminCidrs: ['0.0.0.0/0'] for dev, against 203.0.113.0/24 for staging (line 49) and two named ranges for prod (line 62). network-stack.ts:52-58 iterates adminCidrs and adds an ingress rule on tcp/22 for each, so the dev bastion accepts SSH from anywhere. Port 22 is one of the ports INF-04 names as turning this straight into a finding rather than a review item. The bastion security group is also an ingress source for Postgres on 5432 (network-stack.ts:81-85), so the jump host is a path to the database.
findings.impact: The dev bastion is exposed to internet-wide SSH scanning and credential attack, and it holds database reach by design. Compounded by F-BC-04: dev is the environment a bare `cdk deploy` selects.
findings.recommendation: Give dev a real range, or drop the bastion in favour of SSM Session Manager, which needs no ingress rule at all. If an open range is genuinely wanted for developer convenience, make it explicit and time-boxed rather than a value in a config file that a fallback can select.

triage.reason: This is not the public load balancer on 80/443 that INF-04 exempts - it is a management port on a jump host, which the procedure sends straight to a finding.
No NACL, managed firewall or SSM-only policy is declared in this repository; per INF-04, an undeclared one is not to be assumed.
It is not a path that does not ship: it is the default configuration object, and F-BC-04 shows it is what a caller with no BEACON_ENV gets.

findings.title: The environment selector falls back to dev for any unrecognised or missing value
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk pickEnv silently defaults to dev
findings.evidence: environments.ts:82-84 returns `environments[name ?? ''] ?? dev` - so an unset BEACON_ENV, a typo such as 'production' instead of 'prod', or any other unmatched string silently yields the dev configuration. bin/beacon.ts:14 calls it with `process.env.BEACON_ENV ?? app.node.tryGetContext('env')` and the comment on lines 12-13 acknowledges the fallback as intended for a laptop synth. The selected object supplies account and region (line 16), so the fallback also redirects the deployment target to account 000000000001, and it carries adminCidrs 0.0.0.0/0 and assetsPublic true.
findings.impact: A mistyped environment name does not fail - it deploys, quietly, with the most permissive configuration in the file. Combined with F-BC-03 and F-BC-02 the fallback selects internet-wide SSH and a public bucket, and the stack names are also derived from cfg.name (bin/beacon.ts:18-27), so the mistake is visible only to someone reading the synthesized stack names.
findings.recommendation: Throw on an unrecognised or missing environment name. If a laptop synth needs a default, make it an explicit `BEACON_ENV=dev` in the developer instructions rather than a silent fallback in the selector.

triage.reason: The fallback is in the shipped selector that every entry point calls; there is no build-time or environment gate that removes it.

The intent stated in the comment is bounded to a laptop synth, and nothing enforces that bound - the same code path runs in the pipeline, where an unset variable produces a deploy rather than an error.
The consequence is not merely informational: it selects a different AWS account and a materially weaker security configuration.

findings.title: The artifact grant is issued with no prefix, defeating the scoping the helper was built for
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk grantArtifacts called without the prefix parameter
findings.evidence: service-role.ts:48-51 documents the contract: "Pass the prefix the service writes under so the grant stays scoped to it", and the signature defaults prefix to '' (line 55). api-stack.ts:39 calls grantArtifacts(serviceRole.role, props.artifacts.bucket) with two arguments, so the default applies and the statements resolve to arnForObjects('*') for GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject and an s3:prefix condition of '*' for ListBucket (lines 57-69). Per data-stack.ts:26-27 that bucket holds brand assets, rendered documents and tenant exports together.
findings.impact: The API task role can read, overwrite and DELETE every object in the shared bucket, including other services' rendered documents and every tenant's exports. The parameter that exists to prevent exactly this is silently defaulted away, so the code reads as scoped and is not.
findings.recommendation: Make prefix a required parameter so a call site cannot omit it, and pass the API's own prefix at api-stack.ts:39. Requiring it is what turns the docstring into a control.

triage.reason: The scoping mechanism is the prefix parameter itself, and it is not applied; no bucket policy in bucket.ts narrows what a principal with s3:* on the objects may do.
The service legitimately needs its own prefix, which is what bounds the intended access; the grant is not bounded to it.
This is not absent defence in depth - it is the primary access control on the objects, and F-BC-02 shows the layer around it is public rather than restrictive.

findings.title: The production database is declared publicly accessible
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk RDS publiclyAccessible true
findings.evidence: data-stack.ts:58-60 sets publiclyAccessible: true with the comment "The analytics warehouse lives in a separate account and pulls nightly over the public endpoint" - so a publicly resolvable endpoint is the stated intent. It sits alongside vpcSubnets PRIVATE_ISOLATED (line 48) and securityGroups [databaseSg] (line 49), and network-stack.ts:71-85 admits only serviceSg and bastionSg on 5432. The declaration and the placement contradict each other.
findings.impact: The instance is declared as wanting an internet-routable endpoint for a Postgres port. Two controls currently stand in the way, which is why this is probable rather than confirmed: PRIVATE_ISOLATED subnets have no internet gateway route, so a public IP would not be routable, and the security group admits only two named groups. The finding is that the intent recorded in the code is to expose the database, so a later change to either control - a subnet retype, a CIDR ingress rule for the warehouse account - removes the protection without touching this line, and nothing here would flag it.
findings.recommendation: Set publiclyAccessible: false and give the analytics account a VPC peering connection, PrivateLink endpoint or a cross-account read replica. If a public endpoint is genuinely required, make the security group ingress the explicit, reviewed control and pin it to the warehouse's addresses.

triage.reason: Two compensating controls are enforced in layers a caller cannot skip: PRIVATE_ISOLATED subnets (data-stack.ts:48) have no IGW route, and databaseSg (network-stack.ts:71-85) admits only serviceSg and bastionSg on 5432. Per triage.md a rule that HOLDS rules the finding out - which is why this is not reported as an exposed database. It is reported as probable and medium because what survives is different: the declared configuration asks for exposure and the protection is entirely incidental to two settings in another file.
The intent is bounded to one analytics account, but publiclyAccessible is not a per-peer setting - it bounds nothing.
An organizational SCP or config rule that forbids publicly accessible RDS instances would settle this, and none accompanies the repository.

findings.title: The API container is configured with a wildcard CORS origin and credentials enabled
findings.unaided_label: beacon-cdk CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN=* with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=true
findings.evidence: api-stack.ts:53-61 sets CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN to '*' and CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS to 'true' in the container environment, with the comment at lines 57-58 explaining that the origin cannot be pinned because tenants use their own subdomains. This is the pairing WEB-16 names: a wildcard origin with credentials. Browsers reject the literal combination, so the usual implementation response - and the one the neighbouring edge-relay service in this tree actually took, reflecting $http_origin (F-ER-04) - is to reflect the caller's Origin, which is unbounded.
findings.impact: If the image reflects the origin, any web page can read authenticated API responses cross-origin with the victim's credentials; if it emits the literal wildcard, credentialed cross-origin requests fail and the tenant subdomain use case is broken. Either outcome is a defect, and the configuration cannot express what the comment wants.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with an anchored allowlist pattern for the tenant subdomain space and have the application match the Origin against it in full before reflecting. The requirement described in the comment is satisfiable; the value configured here does not satisfy it.

triage.reason: The consuming image is beacon/api:1.12.0 (api-stack.ts:50) and its source is not in this tree, so how it interprets these two variables together cannot be established here. Per triage.md this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is the status reported.
The values are configuration constants set in the task definition, so they are not attacker-controlled - but the exposure they configure is what is asserted, and the wildcard is present as written.
The API is credentialed by the same configuration (CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS), so its responses are per-user rather than identical for everyone.
